name: Sarcosine (hair)

lead: Sarcosine is a small naturally occurring amino acid, an N-methyl form of glycine. It is listed as a component in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle energy and cells for fuller-looking hair.
In the body it is an intermediate in choline-to-glycine metabolism. No clinical study of sarcosine for hair growth was found.

paras: It is encountered as one listed ingredient in topical or supplement blends used as part of a regular hair routine.
No hair-specific safety data were described in the sources reviewed. Its sarcosinate derivatives are widely used as surfactants in consumer products.

angle.text: Sarcosine is a glycine-derived amino acid listed in some hair-growth blends, with the idea that it supports follicle cells and energy for fuller-looking hair. Hair studies behind it were not found.

lead: Sarcosine, also called N-methylglycine, is a naturally occurring amino acid derivative that appears as an ingredient in some hair-growth and hair-care blends. The appearance idea behind it is that supporting follicle metabolism or scalp conditions might help hair look fuller, though the product claims rest on ingredient-level reasoning rather than on trials of sarcosine for hair.[1]

Chemically it is the N-methyl derivative of glycine and occurs in muscle and other tissues as an intermediate in the conversion of choline to glycine.[1] A 2023 review of glycine and ageing notes that the enzyme GNMT methylates glycine to form sarcosine and that sarcosine levels decline with age.[2] A 2025 Nature Aging paper reports that sarcosine decreases in sarcopenia and examines its effects on muscle regeneration in anti-inflammatory macrophages.[3]

No published human study has tested sarcosine itself for hair growth. A related but different compound, N,N-dimethylglycine sodium salt (DMG-Na), has been studied in pattern hair loss, including a 2025 24-week double-blind randomized trial of a topical DMG-Na and caffeine product.[4]

paras: Sarcosine (C3H7NO2) is a colourless, highly water-soluble crystalline solid that exists as a zwitterion at neutral pH. Justus von Liebig first isolated it in 1847. It is present in human blood at low micromolar levels.[1]

Sarcosine is formed when glycine N-methyltransferase transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to glycine, a step that helps clear methionine; the 2023 review describes sarcosine as declining with age.[2] It acts on the glycine transporter GlyT1 and NMDA receptor signalling, which is why trials in schizophrenia used 2 g/day add-on sarcosine, a setting unrelated to hair.[1][5]
In a 2025 Nature Aging study, sarcosine was reported to fall in sarcopenia and to enhance muscle regeneration and adipose thermogenesis via anti-inflammatory macrophages.[3]

Sarcosine is used to make biodegradable surfactants such as sodium lauroyl sarcosinate, which appear in toothpaste and other products, and as a reagent in organic synthesis.[1] Research outside hair care has examined its action on the glycine transporter GlyT1 and NMDA receptors, with early studies in schizophrenia and rodent models of depression, and a debated role as a prostate cancer biomarker.[1]

No studies found of sarcosine for hair growth. Human trials of sarcosine have examined schizophrenia, including a 6-week double-blind trial of 60 patients comparing sarcosine and D-serine add-on treatment.[5]

The nearby compound N,N-dimethylglycine sodium salt has been tested in pattern hair loss, including a 24-week double-blind placebo-controlled trial of a topical DMG-Na and caffeine formulation published in 2025 and a 2026 study on dermal papilla senescence; these concern DMG-Na, not sarcosine.[4][6]
